articles.text: We had intended giving the morning report of the Chicago convention but the wires are not working well and outside of the fact that Gen. J. D. Henderson, of St. Louis, is permanent chairman no further report has been received. Arthur and Blaine are still leading, with Harrison and Gresham as prominent rivals in case the strength of the leaders neutralize each other.
articles.summary: The wires being poor, the paper reports only that Gen. J. D. Henderson is permanent chairman of the Chicago convention and that Arthur and Blaine lead.

articles.text: We are glad to see the determined fight that the Glendive Times is waging with the corrupt Custer county ring. That county is now about $120,000 in debt and has scarcely been organized a year and a half. The result is excessive taxation and citizens are getting discouraged and cattle men especially are leaving. There is and can be no excuse for this state of affairs. It is stealing, pure and simple. On top of all this, the ring is preparing to foist a new paper on the citizens of Glendive. It is supposed to be the defunct Fargo Broadaxe outfit and will soon die in Glendive. The reason for its establishment is that an election is coming on and the ring wants an organ. If the citizens of Glendive support the new journal, they will be harming themselves more than they know. Neither Glendive or any other town of its size can support two papers. It is far better to have one live, energetic paper like the Times, than two or more half-starved sheets which are only a drag on the town. As the movement to start the new paper is undoubtedly a piece of spite work to ruin a paper that has refused to quietly stand by and see the county plundered, there is still less reason that any support should be given it. We are the more free in speaking of Custer county affairs as we do not think that there is any danger of such a ring ever gaining control in Billings county. We wish it distinctly understood that any attempt of the kind will be saluted by a broadside in the COW BOY that will open the eyes of the tax-payers. Billings can and will have a clean county administration. Almost invariably a number of bumming place seekers and political shysters get hold of the county reins at first. Billings county is to be an exception or there will be music in the air.
articles.summary: Packard backs the Glendive Times against the 'corrupt Custer county ring' and its planned new paper, and warns that any such ring in Billings county will be exposed by the Cow Boy.

articles.text: Were there really any danger that Pat Donan would be appointed governor, there would be a popular uprising very much resembling civil war, in Dakota. That such an uncollapsable windbag should even be mentioned as a candidate is a standing disgrace to our Territory.
articles.summary: The paper calls Pat Donan an 'uncollapsable windbag' whose mention as a candidate for territorial governor is a disgrace.

articles.text: "Like angels' visits," few and far between, is the meeting of two cremationists. The ideas are too new and their adherents too scattered for much organization. For this reason, it is a real pleasure which we have never experienced but once, to meet a pronounced adherent of the cause. Mr. Julius LeMoyne, of Washington, Pa., referred to in our local columns, is at present the leading cremationist of the United States. The only crematory in this country is now owned by him and was built by his father. We do not now propose to enter into a discussion of the merits of cremation, but wish to say that four-fifths of the cremationists in the United States were made such by a thorough, practical understanding of the subject by the successful operation of the LeMoyne crematory. We are glad to see that the tide of public opinion, as shown by many newspaper articles, is turning in favor of cremation. Leading scientific men everywhere are coming to regard it as altogether the most preferable way of disposing of bodies and the only way to protect the living from contagion by the dead. Before the next generation has passed away, burial will be considered almost as barbarous as was cremation when LeMoyne began his crusade.
articles.summary: Packard, himself a cremationist, welcomes Julius LeMoyne of Washington, Pa., owner of the only crematory in the country, and predicts burial will come to seem barbarous.

articles.text: Especial attention is called to the notice published in another column in reference to persons setting the grass on fire. The move is one in the right direction and cattlemen mean busines in offering the reward. Grass is their source of profit and no effort will be spared to punish the carelessness or criminality of any one destroying it. There are stringent United States and Territorial laws against setting fire to the grass and any one found doing so can make up his mind to suffer to the full extent of the law.
articles.summary: The paper calls attention to the cattlemen's reward for information on persons setting the grass on fire.

articles.text: Considerable comment was caused yesterday by the reported receipt of a telegram that Star & Bullock had telegraphed their intention of shipping by the way of Pierre. The facts in the case are as follows: Star & Bullock have their orders in for goods months ahead. Up to the time when the route was established from here all their goods were consigned by the way of Pierre. Upon the establishment of the Medora route, all their goods were ordered this way. The most of them had already been marked by way of Pierre, and re-marked by way of Medora. The consignment now at Pierre is one of these lots, which was not re-directed. The telegram which was received here was from Star & Bullock to the forwarding company and was to the effect that the lot of goods at Pierre was needed immediately and requested that John Sechler's outfit should be loaded with what freight of theirs was here so that he could go to Pierre. This is all there is to the numerous and conflicting reports circulated yesterday which all seemed to lean toward the opinion that Star & Bullock had abandoned our route. It would be well to examine the reliability of the reports hereafter, before giving them credence.
articles.summary: The paper explains that a telegram from Star & Bullock about goods at Pierre did not mean the firm had abandoned the Medora freight route.

articles.text: Stock and feeding cattle are at least $1 per hundred weight higher, relatively, than they were a year ago. This narrows the margin of feeders. The liberal profits and quick returns of feeding and the great abundance of grass and rough feed have been chief among the causes to bring this about.—[Drovers' News.
articles.summary: Clipped note (Drovers' News) that stock and feeding cattle are about $1 per hundredweight higher than a year ago.

articles.text: The round-up has progressed far more rapidly than was expected and to-day will cross the rail-road at Andrew's creek. Nothing of particular importance has occurred, and the boys seem to be enjoying themselves thoroughly. Some of the Texas cattle from up the river have drifted badly but besides these there are very few ahead of the round-up.
articles.summary: The round-up has moved faster than expected and is to cross the railroad at Andrew's creek today; some Texas cattle have drifted badly.

articles.text: David Neff, near Osborn, O., has a Jumbo of a steer five year old in February; he weighs 2,840 pounds and is far from being fat; in height measures six feet four inches, girths nine feet and is nine feet long from base of horns to root of tail. He is so gentle and kind that the small children play with him, leading him around with an ordinary cow-chain around his neck.—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Clipped note about David Neff's 2,840-pound steer near Osborn, Ohio.

articles.text: To a reporter of the New York Herald Mr Bonner said, speaking of the once celebrated trotter, Dexter: "He is now twenty-six years old, and has been kept at my down-town stables during the winter and given only walking exercise, but it is the intention to drive the old horse on the road during the coming season, as he is full of life and vigor and retains a great deal of his old-time speed."
articles.summary: Clipped note: Robert Bonner says the old trotter Dexter, now twenty-six, is still full of vigor.

articles.text: A remedy for worms in horses is given by a writer of experience in an exchange. He says: "Take a lump of rock mineral salt, from one to ten pounds or more, and put it in the horse's manger. In six days the horse or colt will be free of worms. I have used and prescribed this remedy for many years and it has never failed in any one case, and the horse will improve in health and condition at once."—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped remedy for worms in horses (N. W. L. S. Journal).

articles.text: An exchange tells how to treat balky horses as follows: Take a good, reliable horse—a good puller—and the balky one. Put similar harness on the two, attach them together and start them in opposite directions. At first the balky horse will allow himself to be dragged backwards, but soon he will tire of this and commence to pull in good earnest, and after that he will never refuse to do his duty.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped advice on breaking a balky horse (N. W. L. S. Journal).

articles.text: Dorr Clark, owner of the VVV outfit, and half owner of the E6 brand, is in town, waiting for two hundred head of Short-horn bulls, which will be in Saturday. Mr. Clark is an enthusiastic convert to the thoroughbred bull question and this lot will make about five hundred that he has on his two ranches. He also uses six bulls for every hundred cows. Since his arrivtl here, he has examined the capabilities of the country and thinks, as do all cattle men, that this is the best place in the United states for cattle. To prove his belief, he expects to drive up about 5,000 steers to fatten in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Dorr Clark of the VVV outfit is in town awaiting 200 Short-horn bulls due Saturday and plans to drive about 5,000 steers to fatten in the Bad Lands.

articles.text: The largest cattle herd in Montana owned by one firm or company is that of L. G. Baker & Co., or the Benton & St. Louis Cattle company. Besides the Swett herd recently purchased by C. W. Price and L. G. Baker & Co., Mr. L. C. Baker, of St. Louis, has contracted for the delivery of 2,000 head of two-year-old heifers at the nearest point to Fort Benton, which will make the total owned by this company, estimating the increase for this year, about 25,000 head, of a cash value of not less than $1,000,000. We understand that the company will have $100,000 worth of steers to market this fall. If the Benton & St. Louis Cattle company continue to make purchases as they have during the past two years it will not be long before they can size up with the Swan Land and Cattle company of Wyoming, which is perhaps the largest stock company in the world. The Choteau county company has the advantage of a better range and a better stock country generally, and for that reason will make more rapid progress and earn larger dividends than the other outfit.—[River Press.
articles.summary: Clipped River Press item on the Benton & St. Louis Cattle company's growing Montana herd.

articles.text: Some of our local stock raisers in the southern part of the state, as well as those in the Neutral Strip and Panhandle country, are adopting a new system of handling their local bred cattle which will prevent their home ranges from being overstocked, and protect them from serious loss during very severe winters; which will assure a sufficient amount of grass for winter grazing for all stock left on the local range and prevent the same from being over-crowded. The system they have and are abopting is to have two ranges, one for breeding purposes and the other for maturing their beef cattle on. The last named located in the north, either in Wyoming or Montana, to which they take all steer cattle over the age of one year old, and either drive or ship them to their grazing field in the north and hold them until fully matured before they are marketed. This system not only gives them fatter cattle, but gives them increased weight from two to four hundred pounds to the animal over our local breed steer cattle.—[Ford County (Kan.) Globe.
articles.summary: Clipped Ford County Globe item on southern stockmen keeping separate breeding and northern maturing ranges.

articles.text: Messrs. Julius Le Moyne, of Washington, Pa., Joseph U. Rose, Pittsburgh, W. K. Duval, Wheeling, W. V. and Harvey T. Halleck, Washington, Pa., have been in town several days, arranging to put in cattle on Tepee bottom, under the management of D. K. Wade. A company has been formed and as a starter, six hundred graded cattle have been purchased and will be here in three weeks. Mr. LeMoyne, who is a prominent Short-horn breeder and president of the Washington county Thorough-bred stock association, thinks seriously of deserting his first love and using Polled bulls exclusively. The result of such an experiment would be valuable to our stockmen as it is thought that Polled cattle will stand severe weather better and are otherwise hardier than Short-horns.
articles.summary: Julius LeMoyne and partners from Pennsylvania and West Virginia have formed a company to put 600 graded cattle on Tepee bottom under D. K. Wade.

articles.headline: SPORTING NOTES.
articles.text:
Teemer defeated Conley by a quarter of a length in their single sculll race at Pullman, Decoration day.

On May 28, for the first time on record, the English Derby ended in a draw. St. Gatien and Harvester were the tying horses.

McLaughlin and Dufur will wrestle collar-and-elbow, best two in three, at Buffalo, June 6. The contest is for $500 and gate money.

The record on 75 yards was broken by John S. Barnes, of St. Paul, May 30. The previous record, made by Myers, Lee and others, was 7¾ seconds. Barnes' time was 7 seconds.

Slosson realized the highest expectations of his friends in his contest with Schaeffer at Chicago last Sunday night, and beat the champion, at the balk-line game of billiards. Betting was $125 to $40 on Schaeffer and large sums were laid at these odds.
articles.summary: National sporting briefs: sculling, the drawn English Derby, wrestling, a 75-yard record and billiards.

articles.headline: A Hunted Man.
articles.text: F. C. Leethem, the representative of Marder, Luse & Co., type founders, passed through Glendive on Thursday morning's train, cached behind trunks in a baggage car. He sold some goods at Helena when the authorites got after him for not paying the Territorial license. He learned of this and skipped for the east by the first train. At every town he was searched for but by getting off the cars on the opposite side from the platform and waiting until the train started he escaped. As the train pulled out of the Glendive station he was heard to remark: "Well, this is a h—l of a country." Leethem had no love for cowboys and on his arrival at Medora he got off to see Packard, of the Bad Lands Cowboy, but on seeing some of these famous gentry between him and the hotel, he suddenly concluded that Packard was not at home, or at least that he was not anxious to see him.—[Glendive Times.
articles.summary: Glendive Times story of type-founders' agent F. C. Leethem fleeing a Montana license charge and avoiding Packard at Medora.

articles.headline: Sure Enough Railroad.
articles.text: A Pioneer reporter was on yesterday, permitted to read a letter from one in authority, to a prominent citizen of Deadwood, relative to the construction of the Northern Pacific spur from Medora to this city. The absence of authority from the writer, to publish the letter, alone prevents its appearance in lieu of this article. We do not, however, we think, violate confidence, in stating that abundant assurance is given, not only that the road will be constructed, but that work will begin in a very few days, in fact has already begun if the ordering a survey, and preparing therefor is any portion of the important undertaking. Within a few days at the outside, the project will mature, details will be arranged, and the Pioneer at liberty to disclose full particulars of this most important movement to the entire Hills section. If we can be positive of anything in this world of ours, we may safely count upon all rail communication with the outside world before many moons shall wane.—[Black Hills Pioneer.
articles.summary: Black Hills Pioneer report that a Northern Pacific spur from Medora to Deadwood is assured and work is about to begin.

articles.headline: Six Shooters Among Cattle Men.
articles.text:
At the annual meeting of leading cattle raising associations of Texas in 1882, prompt and very active measures were taken to banish the deadly six-shooter from cattlemen's belt. Resolutions were passed unanimously pledging owners of ranches and cattle not to keep in their employ any hands that would carry deadly weapons. That spring, there was an absence of deadly encounters and shooting sprees observable throughout the range country.

Last year no action was taken by stockmen in convention assembled in regard to the "six-shooter," and since that time serious and deadly shots have been fired. In almost every section of the West murders are on the increase, and cowmen are too often the principal in the encounters. The six-shooter loaded with deadly cartridges is a dangerous companion for any man, especially if he should unfortunately be primed with whisky.

Cattlemen should unite in aiding the enforcement of the law against the carrying of deadly weapons. Lawlessness in any form is hurtful, morally and from a business standpoint, and no business is injured than that of cattle raising, when its employes are allowed to carry deadly weapons. Then we would suggest to the managers of cattle ranches to see that the six-shooter is banished from his outfit.—[Texas L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Texas Live Stock Journal piece urging cattlemen to banish the six-shooter from their outfits.

articles.summary: Tom Tighe came up from Mandan to work for the N. P. at Freyburg.

articles.text: John O'Sullivan has moved his barber shop to this side of the river and is occupying temporary quarters with John Warn.
articles.summary: John O'Sullivan has moved his barber shop across the river, sharing quarters with John Warn.

articles.summary: The round-up is turning up more fat cattle than expected.

articles.text: Mr. Tobin, of Mandan, was in town a day or two last week. He is thinking strongly of entering into a partnership with Tom Stack. It will make a strong partnership and doubtless be successful.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a number of lithograph bird's eye views of Spearfish, from Dr. J. M. Louthan. It is an excellent view and a good advertisement for Spearfish.
articles.summary: Dr. J. M. Louthan sent lithograph bird's-eye views of Spearfish.

articles.text: H. H. Parkins has been here several days learning the system of book-keeping inaugurated by Auditor Kerr. Mr. Parkins will have charge of the Duluth cold-storage house.
articles.summary: H. H. Parkins is learning Auditor Kerr's book-keeping system and will run the Duluth cold-storage house.

articles.text: Several half-breeds were in town Sunday, indulging in unlimited fire-water. One of them was urged to fight the bears on a bet. But the wily half-breed had a level head when he answered: "Liver more wort dan dollars."
articles.summary: Several half-breeds drinking in town Sunday; one declined a bet to fight the bears.

articles.text: A number of persons have taken advantage of our agency and subscribed for outside papers and periodicals. Subscriptions at regular publishers rates will be received for any paper or periodical published in the world.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office takes subscriptions for outside papers and periodicals.

articles.text: Notice is again given that Dr. E. E. Ball, an experienbed dentist of Mandan, will be here the 9th, 10th and 11th, prepared to do any work in his line. A call on the dentist at this time is likely to save much suffering when one is not near.
articles.summary: Dr. E. E. Ball, dentist of Mandan, will be in Medora June 9-11.

articles.text: A coal-mine has been located and opened in the bluff east of town. Superior coal has been found in it, the vein being about eight feet thick. The citizens of Medora can rely on getting a fine quality of coal at a cheap rate the coming winter.
articles.summary: A coal-mine with an eight-foot vein has been opened in the bluff east of town.

articles.text: Work is going forward rapidly on a new side track. It will run on the south side of the main track, beginning several hundred yards east of the depot. A new freight house for the rail-road company will be built at the same time.
articles.summary: A new side track and freight house are under construction east of the depot.

articles.text: A fatal mistake was providentially discovered Monday by the keen eye of Uncle John. A bone man had nearly finished his load when one of a rather odd shape attracted the attention of the aforesaid eagle eye. It, the bone, was immediate[ly?] dragged out and the voice of our esteemed fellow citizen, Mr. Thomas Stack was heard coming from it, in thanksgiving for his delivery.
articles.summary: Humorous item: 'Uncle John' rescued Thomas Stack from a bone man's load on Monday.

articles.text: The second kiln of brick, which will be ready for burning in a few days, is to contain over 200,000. A permanent kiln is to be erected immediately, thus saving much waste. Specimens of the brick at the COW BOY office have been examined by many competent judges and unanimously pronounced equal to any brick made.
articles.summary: The second brick kiln will hold over 200,000 brick and a permanent kiln is to be built.

articles.text: John Bruguier, a well-known scout, is in camp across the track. Johnny is known and liked all over the northwest. To his efficient services, General Miles willingly concedes that he owes his promotion. Strange to say Johnny is as great a favorite with the Indians as with the soldiers. Were it not for him the Sioux would not have come in, and Sitting Bull would still be "bordering" on the Canadian line, making hostile incursions into this country instead of living peaceably with his tribe at Standing Rock. Through his intercession, also Chief Joseph and the Nez Perces surrendered. In these wars he was the constant friend of the white men. During the Nez Perce war he made one of the fastest long-distance rides on record with dispatches from Fort Keogh to Bismarck. The distance is 300 miles and he made it in just thirty-two hours. John's father was French and his mother an Indian. Johnny himself is married to the prettiest squaw in Sitting Bull's tribe.
articles.summary: Scout John Bruguier, credited with bringing in Sitting Bull's Sioux, is camped across the track.

articles.text: The American lacrosse team has so far whitewashed its opponents in England.
articles.summary: The American lacrosse team is unbeaten in England.

articles.text: A party of Yankton Indians is in camp on the south side of the track. We did not look at the teeth of the patriarch but should judge that he was about four hundred and steen years old, perhaps four hundred and umpty. Conversation was voluble on the Yankton side of the house, between bites at a bone which had seen its palmiest days long before even the pigs had given it up at the slaughter-house. The old man isn't bigger than a minute and he is weighted down with a log chain to keep the wind from blowing him away.
articles.summary: A party of Yankton Indians is camped south of the track.

articles.text: Word has come from Belfield that in addition to the horses already stolen there, two horses and six mules were stolen last Friday evening. The grass raising in the morning, completely hid the trail and it was impossible to tell even in what direction the thieves went. Telegrams were sent in every direction, but no word has been received as yet in reference to any of the stolen stock. The loss falls heavily on some of the citizens of Belfield and it is to be hoped that the stock will be recovered and the thieves summarily punished.
articles.summary: Two horses and six mules were stolen at Belfield last Friday evening; the trail was lost.

articles.text:
W. M. Farrow, who was with the victorious American team, when they defeated the Irish team at Dollymount in 1880, and who is one of the best, if not the best off-hand rifle shot in the world, gave an exhibition of his skill at 200 yards, in Little Missouri last Sunday afternoon. He used a new Bullard repeating rifle, 40-75. The target was an 8-inch bull's-eye, with circles two inches apart, the count in the bull's-eye being 11, and 12 for the centre.

SCORE.
10, 10, 11, 11, 11, 11, 10, 10, 10, 12,—106.

This fine score was made with hunting ammunition and without cleaning the rifle. All the bullets were planted inside a 12-inch circle.
articles.summary: Champion marksman W. M. Farrow gave a 200-yard rifle exhibition in Little Missouri last Sunday, scoring 106.

articles.headline: NOTICE OF DISSOLUTION.
articles.text: TO ALL WHOM IT MAY CONCERN: Be it known that on and after this 24th day of May, 1884, the partnership heretofore existing between Chas. Shaffer and John Munroe, under the firm name of Shaffer & Munroe, Plum Grove ranch, on the Little Missouri river, is dissolved by mutual consent. All indebtedness of the firm to date will be paid by John Munroe.
articles.summary: Shaffer & Munroe of Plum Grove ranch dissolved their partnership as of May 24, 1884.
